clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: Female patient with idiopathic membranous nephropathy on heavy immunosuppression (prednisolone, mizoribine, cyclosporine) presented with sudden severe epigastric pain on Day 77. Given the known final diagnosis of VDVZV (varicella-zoster virus disseminated disease), the trajectory likely involves: immunosuppression-related VZV reactivation → visceral involvement (abdominal pain) → cutaneous manifestations (skin lesions by Day 80) → confirmation via serology or PCR.

report.source_text: On the morning of Day 80, a large number of small blisters appeared on the face and trunk, which are characteristic of varicella. Skin lesion biopsy revealed that blisters had formed within the epidermis, and cells with ground-glass nuclei were seen in the blister cavities (Fig. 3). Polymerase chain reaction results were positive for VZV. The blood VZV-DNA numbers had increased markedly.

clinician.current_trajectory_hypothesis: Female patient with idiopathic membranous nephropathy on heavy immunosuppression presented with sudden severe epigastric pain on Day 77 (likely visceral VZV involvement). By Day 80, characteristic varicella vesicles appeared on face and trunk with histopathologic confirmation (ground-glass nuclei in epidermal cells) and positive VZV PCR with elevated blood VZV-DNA. The trajectory supports disseminated VZV (VDVZV) in an immunocompromised host.

report.source_text: Acyclovir (1500 mg/day) and immunoglobulin (5 g/day) were immediately administered intravenously, and the dosages of prednisolone and immunosuppressant were reduced. Liver function further worsened temporarily, disseminated intravascular coagulation was found and treatment was started. The abdominal pain quickly resolved, and the platelet count and liver function improved within 1 week of starting acyclovir. The patient was subsequently discharged.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 23.4 BMI female patient with idiopathic membranous nephropathy (Stage II) was hospitalized in September and treated with heavy immunosuppression (prednisolone 50-60 mg/day, mizoribine 150 mg/day, cyclosporine 150 mg/day). On Day 77 of hospitalization, she developed sudden onset severe epigastric pain without peritoneal signs, with initial imaging showing mild perivascular fat stranding around the celiac artery and superior mesenteric artery (consistent with visceral VZV involvement). Laboratory findings revealed neutrophil-dominant leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymes, and reduced albumin. On Day 80, characteristic varicella vesicles appeared on the face and trunk. Skin biopsy confirmed VZV with intraepidermal blister formation and pathognomonic ground-glass nuclei in blister cavity cells. VZV PCR was positive with markedly elevated blood VZV-DNA. Serology showed prior VZV IgG positivity with VZV IgM negative on Day 80, but seroconversion occurred by Day 86 (VZV IgM positive on paired sera). Acyclovir 1500 mg/day intravenously and immunoglobulin 5 g/day were immediately initiated, with concurrent reduction of prednisolone and immunosuppressants. Abdominal pain resolved rapidly, platelet count and liver function improved within 1 week, and disseminated intravascular coagulation was managed. Patient was subsequently discharged.

Visceral VZV involvement manifesting as sudden severe epigastric pain on Day 77
Cutaneous manifestations of varicella on Day 80
Molecular confirmation of VZV with elevated viral load
Rapid clinical response to antiviral therapy
Management of disseminated intravascular coagulation complication

Known prior history documented as serologically negative for hepatitis B and C virus
